extracted.intended_audience: young authors, literary critics, and readers of philosophical/literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical-maxims for composing and evaluating philosophical and literary prose (symbols, truthfulness, audience, citation/originality, and publication choices). Aimed at authors and critics working in abstruse or speculative genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbols to convey highest ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea, in the highest sense of that word, cannot be conveyed but by a symbol; and, except in geometry, all symbols of necessity involve an apparent contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep or highest ideas should be presented symbolically rather than literally; authors should expect that symbols often entail apparent contradictions. Writings employing such symbolism are not intended for readers 'who could not pierce through this symbolic husk.' (Anti-pattern: forcing literal exposition of the highest ideas; expecting immediate literal clarity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity equals intention to communicate truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Veracity does not consist in saying, but in the intention of communicating, truth; and the philosopher who cannot utter the whole truth without conveying falsehood, and at the same time, perhaps, exciting the most malignant passions, is constrained to express himself either mythically or equivocally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When full literal disclosure would mislead or cause harm, it is acceptable—and sometimes necessary—for an author to express ideas mythically or equivocally. Evaluate honesty by the author's intent to convey truth, not only by literal statements. (Anti-pattern: condemning equivocal or symbolic language as dishonest without considering intent or consequences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding or qualifying answers when personal danger is involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions which cannot be fully answered without exposing the respondent to personal danger, are not entitled to a fair answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics should recognize that some topics cannot be answered candidly for safety reasons; expecting a 'fair' or full answer in such contexts is unreasonable. This affects how one judges completeness or candor in a work. (Scoring note: absence of full disclosure in dangerous contexts should not automatically lower assessment if risk justifies reticence.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style and complexity to anticipated audience
rubrics_metrics.description: That way we would be contented to prove our thesis, which being the worse in itself, is notwithstanding now by reason of common imbecility the fitter and likelier to be brooked. ... pardonably may a writer of the present time anticipate a scanty audience for abstrusest themes, and truths that can neither be communicated nor received without effort of thought, as well as patience of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should judge whether to simplify or temper their arguments to reach a broader audience; it can be permissible to present a less rigorous (but more palatable) thesis if the intended readership cannot absorb abstruse material. Conversely, for specialized readers, retain complexity. (Anti-pattern: refusing to adapt at all and expecting mass comprehension of highly abstruse exposition.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and require reader effort for abstruse material
rubrics_metrics.description: Truths that can neither be communicated nor received without effort of thought, as well as patience of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating abstruse subjects, authors should expect a limited audience and the need for reader effort; clarity, patient exposition, and signals to alert readers to necessary effort are part of good practice. (Evaluation: assign credit for works that properly scaffold difficult ideas and warn readers of the required effort.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of thought/phrase is not proof of plagiarism; nuanced citation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An identity of thought, or even similarity of phrase will not at all times be a certain proof that the passage has been borrowed from Schelling. ... For readers in general, let whatever shall be found in this or any future work of mine, that resembles, or coincides with, the doctrines of my German predecessor, though contemporary, be wholly attributed to him: provided, that the absence of distinct references to his books, which I could not at all times make with truth as designating citations or thoughts actually derived from him; be not charged on me as an ungenerous concealment or intentional plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating originality requires tests beyond superficial similarity or dates; authors should acknowledge intellectual debts when appropriate, but lack of explicit citation (for example, because the author lacked access) should not automatically imply bad faith. Critics should use deeper analysis to determine whether ideas were truly borrowed. (Anti-pattern: equating any resemblance in phrase or idea with deliberate plagiarism.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not avoid intellectual difficulties by willful ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: It teaches us to escape from a difficulty by shutting our eyes: but eyes were made to be open and not to be shut,— except for the sake of rest; when we unclose them again there is the same difficulty, staring us full in the face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics should confront difficulties of subject matter rather than ignore them or seek refuge in evasive rhetoric. Good writing addresses problems directly and does not rely on willful blindness as a rhetorical strategy. (Anti-pattern: deliberately avoiding or glossing over key difficulties to make a thesis seem simpler than it is.)
